title: How Buckingham prepared charts and ran rundowns and takes
summary: He brought printed charts, marked fills, recorded rundowns and usually got the take within one to three tries.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: You had to have perfect relative pitch. If you hear the note, then you know the next note is a 4 or a 6 minor or whatever. You’d write your own charts out. I never did that with the players when I produced. I always did the charts ahead of time with one of my musicians, usually the piano player or the guitar player on whichever session it was. I’d do the charts — I came with them printed up, put them out in the studio. In the control room, “Here’s your chart, here’s the demo, follow the chart.” And I’d put in little notations like, “The fills on this verse piano.” I’d just write it above, just piano. That meant on that verse the piano fills. Next verse it might be, I don’t know, somebody else fills.
Yeah, you don’t want to fill on a fill.

No, no, no. And everybody knows to stay out of everybody’s way anyway. But I would come in with the number charts in Nashville, and I’d run the demo, play the demo, or sit there with the guitar and play it with whoever is singing, and everybody makes their notes in the chart, where they’re filling. I’d write down and they’d put little notes to themselves — go out to the studio, do a rundown, and I’d always record that. Because sometimes it would be the rundown, and if the chart was right, a lot of times that was the take. Then I’d do a rundown, take one, take two, maybe take three. If it went past that I’d say something’s wrong with the chart. Put it away, I’ll look at it during the lunch break. Next song.
But mostly we got it either on the rundown or take one or take two.
